common_name: Fixation Balansa Clover (Extreme Cold-Hardy Balansa Clover)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill shallowly in late summer to fall; Fixation survives brief exposure to temperatures as low as -14F, well beyond what older balansa cultivars can take.

directions: Fixation is a balansa clover selection bred for cold hardiness well beyond earlier balansa cultivars, surviving brief subzero exposure that would kill most other annual clovers outright. Broadcast or drill the fine seed shallowly into a firm, moist seedbed, since good seed-to-soil contact matters more than planting depth for establishment. Like other balansa types it tolerates brief waterlogging and knits into a dense, low winter canopy that scavenges nitrogen and crowds out cool-season weeds. Mow, roll, or incorporate at early bloom to maximize nitrogen contribution ahead of a following crop.

common_name: Pacer Forage Turnip (Fast-Establishing Turnip-Rape Cover Crop)

planting.note: Sow in late summer, roughly six to ten weeks before the average first fall frost, for fast canopy closure and reliable winterkill in cold climates.

directions: Pacer is a hybrid forage turnip crossed with rape, giving it quicker seedling vigor and leafier top growth than straight turnip-type cover crops. Broadcast or drill the small seed shallowly into a firm, moist seedbed in late summer, since rapid early cover is its main advantage over slower brassica covers. The combination of a fleshy taproot and abundant leaf growth scavenges residual soil nitrogen while smothering emerging weeds through fall. It winterkills with the first hard freezes in most of its range, leaving decomposing residue that feeds soil biology ahead of spring planting; where winters stay mild, mow before it bolts.

planting.note: Sow in early spring or late summer into fall; the cross between tatsoi and pak choi gives it both cold hardiness and heat tolerance beyond either parent alone.

directions: Green Giant combines the glossy, rounded leaf of tatsoi with the thicker, more upright petiole of pak choi, producing a sturdy rosette that resists both bolting and bitterness better than either parent type alone. Direct-sow shallowly and thin plants to 6 to 10 inches for full heads, or grow crowded for cut-and-come-again baby greens. It holds up in both the cool damp of early spring and the heat of late summer, making it a reliable filler crop between main brassica plantings. Harvest whole rosettes or individual outer leaves for stir-fries, soups, and braises.

common_name: Violetta Pak Choi (Purple-Topped Baby Pak Choi)

planting.note: Sow after soil has warmed in spring, or again in late summer for a fall crop; purple pigmentation intensifies in cooler weather.

directions: Violetta is a small, fast-maturing pak choi whose leaf tops darken to a deep violet-purple while the stems and undersides stay bright green, giving it strong visual interest in salad mixes as well as in the garden row. Direct-sow shallowly and thin to 6 to 8 inches for baby heads, harvesting whole plants once they reach a compact, crisp rosette. Flavor is sweet and mild with none of the toughness that can show up in larger pak choi types left too long in the field. Because its purple coloring deepens with cooler temperatures, a fall sowing generally produces the most striking color along with the sweetest flavor.

scientific_name: Brassica rapa subsp. pekinensis 'Wa Wa Tsai'

planting.note: Best as a late-summer sowing for fall harvest to avoid bolting; can also be sown in very early spring where the season is long enough.

directions: Wa Wa Tsai is a miniature napa cabbage that forms a tight, barrel-shaped head only about 9 inches tall, making it a practical choice for small beds or succession plantings where a full-sized Chinese cabbage would be too much plant. Direct-sow shallowly in late summer and thin to 8 to 10 inches, since crowded plants fail to form a dense head. The interior is pale, crisp, and sweet with none of the bitterness that can develop in larger, slower-maturing napa types. Its small stature and relatively quick maturity make it one of the earliest mini napa cabbages to harvest in a fall garden.

planting.note: Sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest; the longer maturity window needs an earlier start than standard green napa cabbage.

directions: Scarlette is a napa-type Chinese cabbage whose outer leaves develop a deep magenta-purple blush over crisp white midribs, giving whole or sliced heads a striking two-tone look that most green napa varieties can't match. Direct-sow shallowly in mid to late summer, allowing the full 70-plus days to maturity, and thin to 10 to 12 inches so heads can fill out properly. The color holds up well in slaws and quick pickles, where the contrast between purple leaf and white vein stays vivid even after dressing. Harvest when heads feel firm and dense, since the color intensifies as the head matures.

common_name: Fort Umpqua Turnip (Purple-Topped White Salad Turnip)

planting.note: Sow in early spring for a summer crop or in late summer for a sweeter fall crop; roots hold their quality in the ground after light frost.

directions: Fort Umpqua produces a classic purple-shouldered, white-bottomed turnip root that stays firm and dense rather than becoming pithy as it sizes up, which gives growers more flexibility on harvest timing than many fast-bolting salad turnips. Direct-sow seed shallowly in loosened soil and thin to 3 to 4 inches, since crowding leads to misshapen roots. Both the root and the tender young greens are good eating, with the root holding a mild, slightly peppery bite that mellows when cooked. A fall sowing timed so roots mature after a light frost generally produces the sweetest flavor.

common_name: Tokyo Silky Sweet Turnip (Japanese Salad Turnip)

planting.note: Sow in early spring or, for the best flavor, in late summer for a fall harvest; roots are best pulled small rather than left to size up.

directions: Tokyo Silky Sweet is a Japanese-type salad turnip bred to be eaten raw, with a smooth, glassy-white root that is crisp, juicy, and notably sweet rather than peppery. Direct-sow shallowly and thin to 3 to 4 inches apart, harvesting roots at about 2 inches across for the best texture before they start to toughen. The tender greens are mild enough to eat raw as well, making the whole plant useful rather than just the root. Like other fast salad turnips, it's best grown in a quick-succession planting schedule rather than left in the ground for long-term storage.

planting.note: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop; longer maturity than spring radishes means an earlier start.

directions: Dragon is a Chinese-type radish whose brilliant red skin wraps a pure white, crisp interior, splitting the difference in size between a quick spring radish and a full daikon. Direct-sow seed about a half inch deep and thin to 4 to 6 inches for roots to size up properly without forking. The flavor stays mild and juicy rather than sharp, which makes it good for both raw snacking and quick pickling, and the color holds up strikingly well when sliced into rounds or julienned. Because it takes longer to mature than a standard breakfast radish, give it the full six weeks before expecting harvestable roots.

common_name: Frizzy Lizzy Mustard (Deeply Toothed Baby-Leaf Mustard Green)

planting.note: Sow in early spring or late summer; fast enough to harvest as a baby-leaf cut in as little as three weeks.

directions: Frizzy Lizzy produces deeply toothed, intensely ruffled mustard leaves that add texture as well as a sharp, peppery bite to a baby-leaf salad mix. Broadcast or sow in close rows and begin cutting at about three weeks for the tenderest baby leaves, or let it grow longer for a spicier, more mature green. It regrows readily after a light cut-and-come-again harvest, giving several pickings from a single sowing in cool weather. The frilled leaf edge also makes it a visually interesting addition to the garden bed, not just the salad bowl.
